Family Health

Understanding HER2-negative breast cancer

Updated: October 5, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

HER2-negative is one part of a breast cancer diagnosis, not a complete description of the disease. It means the tumour does not meet the usual criteria for HER2 overexpression or gene amplification. Treatment also depends on estrogen and progesterone receptors, the cancer’s stage and other features. Some HER2-negative cancers respond to hormone therapy, while others are triple-negative. Understanding these distinctions can make your pathology report and treatment discussions easier to follow.

What does HER2-negative mean?

HER2 stands for human epidermal growth factor receptor 2. It is a protein involved in signals that control cell growth. Some breast cancers make an unusually large amount of HER2, often because their cells have extra copies of the HER2 gene. These cancers are called HER2-positive.

HER2-negative cancers do not meet those positive-test criteria. The term does not necessarily mean there is no HER2 protein at all. Laboratories may describe low or ultralow expression because those finer distinctions can affect treatment in particular settings.

Most breast cancers are HER2-negative. The hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative combination is the most common subtype. Neither the word negative nor the amount of HER2 tells you by itself whether a tumour is small, slow-growing, curable or already spread.

Hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative disease

Breast cancer cells are also tested for estrogen receptors, abbreviated ER, and progesterone receptors, abbreviated PR. These receptors can be present in healthy breast cells as well as cancer cells. A cancer with ER, PR or both is described as hormone receptor–positive, or HR-positive.

Hormone signals can help these cancer cells grow. Endocrine treatment works by reducing estrogen production or interfering with its effects on the tumour. It is different from hormone replacement therapy used for menopausal symptoms.

ER-positive disease is common, and many ER-positive cancers are also PR-positive. The exact amount of receptor staining and other tumour features can matter, so ask the team to interpret the complete report rather than treating every positive result as identical.

In the US SEER display for female breast cancer diagnosed during 2019–2023, about 70% of cases were HR-positive/HER2-negative and about 11% were HR-negative/HER2-negative. Some cases had unknown receptor status. These are population figures from a particular registry period, not a prediction about any individual.

Hormone receptor–negative disease: triple-negative breast cancer

When a breast cancer is negative for ER, PR and HER2, it is called triple-negative breast cancer, or TNBC. It lacks the hormone receptors needed for standard endocrine treatment and does not qualify for the usual treatments directed at HER2-positive disease.

TNBC is less common than HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer. As a group it often grows more quickly and has a greater risk of early recurrence, but its behaviour still depends strongly on stage, response to treatment and individual tumour features.

Triple-negative does not mean untreatable. Chemotherapy, surgery and radiation remain important, and some people are eligible for immunotherapy, PARP inhibitors or antibody–drug conjugates. Eligibility requires more information than the three receptor results.

How the laboratory tests HER2

Once invasive breast cancer is diagnosed, tissue from a biopsy or operation is tested for biomarkers. Often the diagnostic biopsy provides enough tissue, although another sample or repeat testing may be needed in some circumstances.

Immunohistochemistry, or IHC, uses antibodies and staining to assess HER2 protein in tumour cells. The result is reported on a scale from 0 to 3+. In the conventional positive/negative system, 0 and 1+ are negative, 3+ is positive, and 2+ is equivocal rather than a final positive result.

An equivocal result usually needs in situ hybridization, or ISH. FISH is a fluorescent form of this test. Its labelled probes identify copies of the HER2 gene in cells; they do not bind to HER2 protein. This distinction matters because IHC measures protein expression while ISH assesses gene amplification.

An IHC 2+ tumour with a negative ISH result is generally classified as HER2-negative; an amplified result can establish HER2 positivity. Pathologists interpret the complete pattern using laboratory criteria, including unusual or conflicting results. IHC is often the first test, but turnaround and cost depend on the laboratory.

Ask for the actual IHC score and any ISH or FISH result, not just a verbal positive or negative label. These details may become useful later if treatment options change.

Why HER2-low and HER2-ultralow now matter

HER2-low commonly means an IHC score of 1+, or 2+ with a negative ISH result. HER2-ultralow refers to an IHC 0 result that still shows some membrane staining. These descriptions identify small amounts of protein within cancers historically grouped as HER2-negative.

They do not mean every HER2-targeted medicine will work. For example, an antibody–drug conjugate can use the HER2 protein to deliver a cancer-killing payload; that is different from assuming a tumour will benefit from a standard trastuzumab regimen used for HER2-positive disease.

A specific US example is the January 2025 approval of trastuzumab deruxtecan, also called T-DXd or Enhertu, for unresectable or metastatic HR-positive, HER2-low or HER2-ultralow breast cancer that has progressed on one or more endocrine therapies in the metastatic setting, using an approved test.

Other indications have their own requirements. This example does not make T-DXd a routine treatment for every early-stage HER2-negative cancer. Availability, previous therapy, test results and potential adverse effects all require an oncology discussion.

Endocrine medicines for HR-positive disease

Several types of endocrine treatment can be used for HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer. The choice depends on menopausal status, stage, previous treatment and whether the aim is to reduce recurrence risk or control advanced disease. These examples explain the main groups; they are not interchangeable prescriptions.

Tamoxifen, including the brand Soltamox, and toremifene, also called Fareston, are selective estrogen receptor modulators, or SERMs. They interfere with estrogen’s effects in breast tissue. Tamoxifen has uses before and after menopause; toremifene is used in particular postmenopausal settings.

Fulvestrant, also called Faslodex, is a selective estrogen receptor degrader, or SERD. It blocks estrogen receptor signalling and promotes receptor breakdown. Other medicines in the broader estrogen receptor–directed group may be options in advanced disease, sometimes according to additional mutations and previous treatment.

Aromatase inhibitors lower estrogen production. Examples are anastrozole (Arimidex), exemestane (Aromasin) and letrozole (Femara). They are commonly used after menopause. Before menopause, an aromatase inhibitor generally needs effective ovarian suppression alongside it.

Endocrine therapy may be given after surgery to lower recurrence risk, before surgery in selected circumstances, or as part of treatment for recurrent or metastatic disease. Tell the team about side effects and other medicines so that the plan can be adjusted safely.

Ovarian suppression and fertility considerations

Before menopause, the ovaries are a major source of estrogen. Reducing their activity can therefore be part of treating HR-positive breast cancer. This is a separate decision from choosing a medicine that blocks the estrogen receptor.

GnRH agonists, also called LHRH agonists, suppress the hormonal signals that stimulate the ovaries. Examples include goserelin and leuprolide. The suppression from medicines can be temporary, although recovery of ovarian function is not guaranteed in every situation.

Removing both ovaries by surgery, called bilateral oophorectomy, permanently stops their hormone production and causes surgical menopause. The consequences for fertility, symptoms and longer-term health should be discussed before choosing that approach.

Chemotherapy can also damage ovarian function and cause temporary or permanent loss of periods. That effect is not a dependable substitute for prescribed ovarian suppression. A missing period alone does not establish that estrogen production has stopped adequately for the proposed treatment.

If future pregnancy matters to you, ask about fertility preservation before treatment starts where possible. Your oncology and fertility teams can explain options, timing and the need to avoid pregnancy during particular treatments.

Targeted medicines used with or after endocrine treatment

Targeted drugs interfere with particular growth or repair pathways. Some act at the cell surface, while others work inside cells; they do not all work simply by attaching to a surface protein.

CDK4/6 inhibitors slow cell-cycle signalling. Abemaciclib (Verzenio), palbociclib (Ibrance) and ribociclib (Kisqali) are examples used in HR-positive/HER2-negative disease, commonly with endocrine therapy in advanced cancer. Certain drugs also have defined early-stage uses; this is not the same indication for every member of the group.

For example, US approval includes ribociclib with an aromatase inhibitor after surgery for selected stage II or III HR-positive/HER2-negative cancers at high risk of recurrence. Whether an additional drug is worthwhile depends on expected benefit, risks and the actual eligibility criteria.

Alpelisib (Piqray) targets the PI3K pathway. It can be combined with fulvestrant for selected advanced HR-positive/HER2-negative cancers with a PIK3CA mutation after previous endocrine treatment. The mutation result and monitoring requirements, including blood sugar, matter.

Everolimus (Afinitor) inhibits the mTOR pathway, which participates in growth signalling. It can be used with endocrine treatment, such as exemestane, in selected advanced cancers after resistance to earlier treatment. Its role is more specific than a general promise to stop tumour cells and new blood vessels.

This is an explanation of established treatment groups, not a complete catalogue of every current approval. Additional mutation-directed medicines and antibody–drug conjugates may be available. Ask which test result supports each proposed treatment and what alternatives exist.

PARP inhibitors and inherited BRCA changes

BRCA1 and BRCA2 help cells repair damaged DNA. A harmful inherited change in one of these genes can create a weakness that PARP inhibitors exploit by interfering with another DNA repair pathway.

Olaparib (Lynparza) and talazoparib (Talzenna) are examples used for eligible HER2-negative advanced breast cancers with an inherited BRCA mutation. Such cancers may be hormone receptor–positive or triple-negative. Previous treatment and the exact indication determine suitability.

Olaparib also has an adjuvant role for selected high-risk, HER2-negative early breast cancers with a harmful inherited BRCA change after neoadjuvant or adjuvant chemotherapy and local treatment. It is therefore inaccurate to say PARP inhibitors are only used after chemotherapy has failed.

An inherited, or germline, test and a test of changes within the tumour answer different questions. Genetic counselling can help explain the findings, treatment implications and possible relevance to relatives.

Surgery, chemotherapy, radiation and immunotherapy

Many people with early HER2-negative breast cancer have breast-conserving surgery, often called lumpectomy, or mastectomy. Surgery treats disease in the breast and may include assessing nearby lymph nodes. The order of surgery and drug treatment depends on the cancer rather than on HER2 status alone.

Chemotherapy destroys cancer cells or interferes with their division. It may be given before surgery to shrink a tumour, afterward to reduce recurrence risk, or to treat advanced disease. Having HR-positive cancer does not automatically remove the need for chemotherapy, although some people can avoid it after risk assessment.

Radiation uses carefully directed energy to treat cancer cells in a chosen area. It is commonly part of treatment after breast-conserving surgery and may also be recommended after mastectomy or for symptoms from spread, depending on the situation.

Immunotherapy helps the immune system act against cancer. It is an established option for selected triple-negative cancers, but it is not a routine treatment for every HR-positive/HER2-negative cancer. Unusual biomarker findings or a clinical trial may create other possibilities.

How triple-negative treatment is planned

For a small operable TNBC, surgery may come first. For higher-risk early disease, the team may recommend chemotherapy before surgery, sometimes with pembrolizumab (Keytruda), followed by surgery and further treatment. Chemotherapy is not reserved only for a tumour that cannot be removed.

Pembrolizumab is used with chemotherapy before surgery and continued afterward in eligible high-risk early TNBC. The criteria differ from metastatic TNBC, where a PD-L1 result may be required for the pembrolizumab–chemotherapy combination. A rule from one setting should not be applied to the other.

After surgery, the response to prior treatment, remaining cancer, lymph nodes and inherited BRCA findings can influence further drug treatment. Radiation is considered according to the operation and disease extent, not simply because the cancer is triple-negative.

For metastatic TNBC, systemic medicines are central. Options can include chemotherapy, immunotherapy, PARP inhibitors for eligible BRCA-related disease and antibody–drug conjugates. Surgery or radiation may help with particular local problems or symptoms. Clinical trials may offer another route to discuss.

Endocrine treatment does not help a tumour that lacks its hormone targets. However, the absence of ER, PR and HER2 positivity should not be confused with the absence of every possible treatment target.

The other details that shape a treatment plan

The team considers the specific breast cancer type, tumour size, lymph node involvement and whether cancer has reached distant organs. Stage describes extent; grade and related findings help describe how abnormal or active the cells appear.

They also consider whether this is a first diagnosis or a recurrence, what medicines or radiation have already been given, how well those treatments worked and whether side effects limit further use. Relevant mutations, including BRCA1, BRCA2 or changes identified in tumour testing, may open additional options.

Age, overall health, menopausal status, fertility wishes and personal preferences all belong in the discussion. Practical issues such as appointments, costs and support can also affect how a plan is delivered.

HER2 and hormone receptor status can change when cancer returns. If another biopsy is appropriate and feasible, the team may repeat biomarker testing rather than assuming that the original tumour and a recurrence have identical features.

Is HER2-negative better than HER2-positive?

There is no reliable better-or-worse ranking based only on this label. HER2-positive cancers often grow quickly without effective treatment, but HER2-directed medicines have substantially changed their outlook.

Some HR-positive/HER2-negative cancers grow relatively slowly and respond well to endocrine treatment. Other HER2-negative cancers, particularly some triple-negative cancers, can be aggressive. It is misleading to say that all HER2-negative cancers spread more slowly or always have fewer useful options.

For your own outlook, tumour size, nodes, distant spread, grade, receptor pattern, general health and response to treatment are more informative together than any single marker. Ask what the complete diagnosis means for the goal and expected benefit of your treatment.

Understanding survival statistics and outlook

Five-year relative survival compares survival among people with cancer with expected survival in a comparable general population. It is not simply the percentage cured, and it does not mean that someone has only five years to live.

US SEER data for women diagnosed in 2016–2022 report five-year relative survival of 95.8% for HR-positive/HER2-negative disease and 78.7% for triple-negative disease across all stages combined. These averages combine very different situations.

The same dataset shows why stage matters: for triple-negative disease, the estimate is 92.8% when localized, 68.3% with regional spread and 14.9% with distant spread. SEER’s localized, regional and distant groups are not interchangeable with the numbered clinical stages.

Statistics describe groups diagnosed in earlier years. They cannot incorporate every individual characteristic or all benefits from the newest treatments. Outcomes also differ between health systems and populations. Your oncologist can interpret evidence in the context of your stage, treatment response and health.

An HR-positive/HER2-negative diagnosis often has a more favourable population outlook than TNBC, but a broad comparison should not replace an individual conversation. Bring questions about the pathology, treatment choices, follow-up and support; understanding the plan is part of receiving care.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NCI guidance distinguishes hormone receptors, HER2 findings and other tumour features. Treatment depends on the complete diagnosis, prior therapy and setting; HER2-negative disease includes cancers with very different treatment options.

FDA indications establish specific uses for medicines such as T-DXd, ribociclib and olaparib. SEER statistics describe US population outcomes from stated diagnosis years and cannot predict an individual course.

How BeMama can help

Keep a copy of your pathology report and ask the oncology team to explain ER, PR, the HER2 score, stage and any additional tests. BeMama can help you organize questions and support needs, but cannot choose a cancer treatment.

When to seek help

Do not start, stop or substitute cancer medicines based on a general article. Follow your oncology team’s instructions for urgent symptoms and treatment side effects, and ask about fertility and pregnancy precautions before therapy where possible.

Evidence notes updated: October 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • HER2-negative is a biomarker result, not a cancer stage.
  • ER and PR separate HR-positive disease from triple-negative disease.
  • FISH examines gene amplification; IHC examines protein staining.
  • HER2-low or ultralow findings can affect particular treatment choices.
  • Surgery, endocrine treatment, chemotherapy and targeted medicines have different roles.
  • Survival figures need a date, population and stage context.

Frequently asked questions

Does HER2-negative mean triple-negative?

No. Triple-negative means ER-negative, PR-negative and HER2-negative. Many HER2-negative cancers have hormone receptors and can benefit from endocrine treatment.

Is an IHC score of 2+ a positive result?

It is an equivocal result that usually needs ISH testing, such as FISH, to clarify gene amplification. Ask for the final combined interpretation.

Does FISH measure HER2 protein?

No. FISH uses fluorescent probes to assess copies of the HER2 gene. IHC evaluates protein staining.

Can a HER2-negative cancer receive a HER2-directed drug?

Some HER2-low or ultralow cancers meet criteria for a specific antibody–drug conjugate. This does not make every HER2-targeted medicine appropriate, and stage and previous treatment matter.

Must surgery always come before chemotherapy?

No. Drug treatment may come first, especially for certain higher-risk early cancers. The sequence is chosen from the full diagnosis and treatment goals.

Are PARP inhibitors only used when chemotherapy has failed?

No. Olaparib also has a defined role after chemotherapy and local treatment in selected high-risk early HER2-negative cancers with an inherited BRCA change.

Can receptor results change if cancer comes back?

Yes. A repeat biopsy and biomarker testing may be recommended when appropriate because a recurrence may have different features.

Does a five-year survival figure predict how long I will live?

No. Relative survival is a population estimate, not a personal deadline or cure rate. Your stage, health, treatment response and available therapies need separate consideration.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
